text.p: The dollar was down from the session's heady heights by late European trading, but still had a firm tone after a boost from perceptions of slow Japanese economic growth and a widening U.S.-Japan interest rate gap.
The dollar drew strength from the weekend Group of Seven meeting and signs that Japanese investors were becoming keener to channel money abroad, traders said.

"There seems to be a view in Japan they're not going to have huge capital losses by being in overseas assets -- they don't see the yen gaining by too much and they're just going for high yields," said Pat Magill, head of Daiwa Europe's corporate desk.
The dollar hit 111.66 yen intraday, its best level since January 1994. It retreated to 111.52/57 by 1533 GMT but remained well up from late Friday's European level of 110.79/85.

Finance ministers and central bankers from the Group of Seven rich nations met at the weekend and expressed satisfaction with current exchange rates. Analysts said the fact they commented on currencies at all had impressed the market.

"The fact they saw fit to say they were happy with the recent trend was seized upon and it's accelerated the dollar's recent upward grind," said Mark Cliffe, chief international economist at HSBC Markets here.
Other factors also helped depress the yen, which traders said took a pounding from currencies such as sterling, the mark and the Australian dollar.
Japanese Finance Minister Wataru Kubo said at the weekend that he sees the Bank of Japan keeping its easy monetary stance to ensure the country's gradual economic recovery.
Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita said the recent fall in long-term Japanese rates may be reflecting changes in sentiment towards Japan's economic prospects.
Data showed Japan's August industrial production fell 1.9 percent. The market had expected an average 1.5 percent drop.
With the prospect of rising interest rates another factor in the dollar's climb against the yen, analysts said that had also underpinned dollar/mark.

"U.S. interest rates seem to be on an uptrend now coming into next year and the end of this year whereas German rates are fixed or on a downward bias over this time horizon," said Shahab Jalinoos, bond analyst at IBJ International in London.
The dollar was quoted at 1.5262/67 marks by 1545 GMT, off a session peak of 1.5291 -- its highest point since mid-July -- but up from late Friday's European level of 1.5237/42.

New U.S. data proved a mixed bag. U.S. August personal income and spending matched forecasts with 0.6 percent rises in both, while August new home sales overshot expectations and the September Chicago purchasing managers' index fell from August.
Single-family home sales increased by 4.7 percent to an annual rate of 832,000 units, the highest rate since April 1996.
The PMI came in at 56.3, down from August's 60.0, although analysts noted in the breakdown that the prices paid index shot up to 59.3 from 51.8 in the previous month.
That warned of a possible pick-up in the region's inflationary pressures, analysts said.
The market's major preoccupation this week is the release of U.S. September non-farm payrolls figures, due out on Friday.

Before that, however, come a variety of U.S. indicators which should grab some market attention. The September NAPM survey and August leading indicators appear tomorrow, while August construction spending is due Wednesday and weekly jobless claims and August factory goods on Thursday.
Elsewhere, sterling set a new 1996 high of 2.3900 marks during the session and stood at 2.3887/02 by 1612 GMT. It made little headway against the buoyant dollar.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44 171 542 8968
